newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish bikers plead not guilty to airport killing.
newsitem.headline: Danish bikers plead not guilty to airport killing.

text.p: Six members and associates of the Hell's Angels bike gang went on trial for murder on Monday, amid the tightest security measures seen in a Danish court.
They were accused of killing a rival in an airport shooting that touched off gang war across the Nordic region.
Brought smiling and joking into court by heavily-armed police in bullet-proof vests, the men denied murdering Bandidos gang leader Uffe Larsen or wounding three of his companions.

The March 10 shooting turned a festering vendetta between the Hell's Angels and the Bandidos into full-blooded war in which the two rivals blasted each other with machineguns, hand grenades, bombs and anti-tank missiles.
Defence lawyers said that their clients, four Hell's Angels and two men described by police as "moving in gang circles" denied being at the airport during the incident.
Prosecutor Bitte Dyrberg said that the six jointly planned the attack and were all guilty of murder and attempted murder, regardless of who fired the shots.

Police, who have long struggled to prove that the gangs are organised criminal rings rather than groupings of errant individuals, hope evidence arising during the proceedings will confirm their claim.
Dyrberg said that sightings of three cars connected to the defendants at the airport and logs of mobile telephone and electronic pager traffic placed them at the scene.
As the case opened, the defence submitted last-minute evidence, to be examined by the prosecution on Tuesday while the court is adjourned.
No details of the new material were available.

Spectators at the courtroom on Monday were screened by a metal detector and scrutinised by officers familiar with biker gangs. Police bomb experts swept the court before the opening session and will do so before each sitting.
Police with automatic rifles at the ready patrolled inside and outside the court complex and the accused were sped to and from the hearing in separate police vehicles.
The biker feud claimed its first life in February 1994, when a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight with Bandidos in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.
Two more Bandidos died over the following two years, in Sweden and in Finland. But the airport incident in March injected new intensity into the bitter feuding.
Gunmen outside Copenhagen International airport shot dead Larsen and wounded three of his companions as they waited to meet fellow-members returning from a visit to Helsinki.
At almost the same time, in Norway, an attacker shot and wounded a Bandido arriving at Oslo's Fornebu airport. Police arrested a member of a Hell's Angels-allied gang.
Since then the weapons used have become heavier, three more people have died and others have been maimed.
The Copenhagen trial, expected to last until December 20, resumes on Wednesday.

The Hell's Angels on Monday launched another case, claiming 2.5 million Danish crowns ($432,200) from police in compensation for a textile business run from a building sealed off as part of a government and police clampdown on the bike gangs.
It produced clothing with the Hell's Angels death's head symbol for the gang's chain of prisoners' aid shops. ($1=5.785 Danish Crown)
